### 2026-11-01: # Schematic design

**5h**

# Schematic design
The circuit schematic was the first step in creating pixelixx, and before i could start, I needed to figure out which components I would need to use

![2026-11-01-22-04-02](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/Enz5eN54l9lqazRN1RmXsVG67e54hcBG/5bc6fa89256ea5269092df96be277d12d2d51a7829b48fc126fcfe67fa557f3d.png)

![2026-11-01-22-04-06](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/Enz5eN54l9lqazRN1RmXsVG67e54hcBG/e4aeae26aa44c877d73260b562dc38be3017e839f882d616f5b9806a1ab9e28b.png)

![2026-11-01-22-04-09](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/Enz5eN54l9lqazRN1RmXsVG67e54hcBG/b068ecfdd9110120ce3c44e9893d2c0db191398ada135823074381148364f114.png)

![2026-11-01-22-04-15](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/Enz5eN54l9lqazRN1RmXsVG67e54hcBG/c3339405ce9888851f179f72d8dfc658292be5c17d0d8699887a40efeb77eb40.png)

![2026-11-01-22-04-19](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/Enz5eN54l9lqazRN1RmXsVG67e54hcBG/914c331cf3fa62084bafc9e48beb7cc51b4c5fbb175b5c6d099edbdcf748c598.png)

. it's build around an esp32-s3-devkitc-1-n16r8, which is the main controller and is responsible for processing data and handling user input. using it as a plug in module simplified things for the pcb.

there are several functional sections of the pcb:
- Microcontroller interface: Two 1×22 connectors provide connections to the ESP32-S3 development board. I assigned GPIO connections for the microphone, LED data output, rotary encoder, and mode-selection button.
- Audio input: A six-pin connector interfaces with an INMP441 I²S microphone module. It provides power, ground, bit clock, word select, and serial data connections.
- LED output: A three-pin connector provides power, ground, and data connections to the external WS2812B LED matrix.
- Power input: A separate two-pin connector supplies external 5V power to the LED matrix.
- Signal conditioning: A 74AHCT125 buffer translates the ESP32's 3.3V logic signal into a suitable signal for the 5V-powered LED matrix. A 330Ω resistor is included in series with the LED data line.
- Power filtering: A 1000µF electrolytic capacitor and a 100nF ceramic capacitor are included across the LED power supply to help reduce supply fluctuations and high-frequency noise.

One important design consideration was separating the LED matrix's power supply from the ESP32's USB power. The LED matrix can draw considerably more current than the development board can provide, particularly when many LEDs are illuminated. Instead, the matrix receives power from a dedicated external 5V supply, while both systems share a common ground.

I also had to consider how KiCad represents power connections and multi-unit components. The 74AHCT125 contains several independent buffer gates, so I needed to account for unused inputs and ensure they were not left floating. I used hierarchical net labels to keep connections understandable and make the schematic easier to follow.

After connecting the components, assigning footprints, and checking the electrical rules, I reviewed the schematic for connectivity problems and inconsistencies. This gave me a circuit design that could be translated into a physical PCB layout.

After completing the schematic, I began translating the circuit into a physical printed circuit board. The objective was to create a compact carrier PCB that could connect the ESP32-S3 development board to the microphone, LED matrix, power supply, and user controls.

I started by transferring the schematic into KiCad's PCB Editor and assigning physical footprints to the components. This included two 1×22 connectors for the ESP32-S3 development board, smaller connectors for the microphone and LED matrix, a screw terminal for external power, and footprints for the resistors, capacitors, and 74AHCT125 IC.

One of the first challenges was getting the ESP32-S3 connectors positioned correctly. Since the development board plugs directly into these connectors, their spacing and alignment are critical. I used the board's mechanical dimensions as a reference to establish the distance between the two header rows. An incorrect spacing would prevent the development board from fitting onto the PCB.

Once the major connectors were positioned, I arranged the remaining components around them. I considered accessibility, component clearance, and the physical connections that would need to be made during assembly. For example, the external power connector needed to remain accessible, while the signal-conditioning and power-filtering components needed to be placed near the relevant connections.

After completing the routing, I ran KiCad's Design Rules Checker (DRC). The final check reported zero unconnected items and zero design-rule violations. Took 6 tries, but it was worth it :)
